https://www.baltictimes.com/taro__over_o.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Taro: Over one million individuals need to be added to the Schengen blacklist 2026-07-23 BNS/TBT Staff TALLINN – The European Union's attempts to restrict the issuance of tourist visas to Russian citizens are not hopeless, even though some member states continue to grant them, said Minister of the Interior Igor Taro (Eesti 200), adding that Estonia's consistent pressure has led to a shift in both the rhetoric of member states and the stance of the European Commission. "I wouldn't want to say it's hopeless, because otherwise there would be no point in doing anything," Taro said on the Kuku radio program "Sihik," commenting on a discussion held a week ago in Dublin at a meeting of EU interior ministers. According to him, Estonia ceased issuing tourist visas to Russian citizens immediately after Russia launched its full-scale aggression in Ukraine and also denies entry to Russian citizens who hold tourist visas issued by any other Schengen country. "Estonia does not let them in: they are formally denied entry and sent back," the minister said, adding that this policy applies at both land borders and airports. Taro emphasized that Estonia's position has been clear from the start. "You cannot come to enjoy the Tallinn Christmas market while your country is bombing Ukraine." ESTONIA PRESSURES THE EU The minister noted that Estonia has consistently raised the visa issue at meetings of EU interior ministers. He said it was concerning that according to last year's Schengen barometer, nearly half a million visas were issued to Russian citizens in eight months, and the trend was increasing. "I said that this is completely unacceptable," Taro recalled. He explained that Estonia's criticism initially met with resistance from countries that issue the most visas, but their tone has since changed. "Their rhetoric has changed somewhat. It has become more apologetic; they claim that they are, in fact, conducting individual risk assessments," the minister said. However, he stressed that the problem has not gone away. "Ukrainians are dying every day, and you are letting Russian citizens travel just for fun, because the Kremlin's goal is to show that nothing significant has happened." ESTONIA WANTS TO EXPAND THE BLACKLIST According to Taro, there is a general consensus within the European Union that visas should not be issued to military personnel involved in Russia's aggression. "I have not yet heard a representative of any country say that this is not the right thing to do," he said. According to the minister, the discussion is primarily about which legal solution would be most suitable for different countries. Estonia's solution, Taro said, is to place individuals associated with the aggression on the Schengen blacklist. He noted that Estonia has already added thousands of names, with support expressed by Latvia, Lithuania, the Czech Republic, Finland, Sweden, and Poland. "We can add hundreds to the list with a single signature," the minister said, explaining that in some countries, adding each name requires a separate ministerial decision. In his view, the actual task is much larger. "We really don't need to add thousands to the list, but hundreds of thousands. In fact, there are over a million of them." Photograph: Richard Drew/AP New York Captain charged after woman and her five-month-old die in New York boat capsizing Manuel Hernandez charged with 13 counts of reckless endangerment after boat overturned in New York harbor Eric Berger Sun 9 Aug 2026 10.47 EDT Last modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 13.28 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The captain of a boat that capsized in the New York harbor on Saturday evening has been charged following the deaths of a 27-year-old woman and her five-month-old daughter. Manuel Hernandez, 46, was arrested and charged with 13 counts of reckless endangerment in the early hours of Sunday morning, a New York police department spokesperson told the Guardian. Police responded to a 911 call at 10.25pm by deploying a helicopter unit to the scene, where divers then found the woman and baby in the water, the spokesperson said. The two victims, whom the NYPD named as Sara Sanchez and her daughter Antonella, were then transported in critical condition to NYU Langone hospital in Brooklyn, where they were pronounced dead. “On Saturday, August 8, 2026, at approximately 2225 hours, police received a 911 call reporting an overturned vessel in the vicinity of Liberty Island, within the confines of the 1st Precinct,” the NYPD said. “The NYPD’s Harbor Unit, SCUBA Team and Aviation responded to the scene.” A dozen other people were rescued from the vessel before the police arrived, and later transported to hospitals, according to the spokesperson. “We are deeply saddened by the tragic loss of life last night, and our thoughts are with the victims’ family and loved ones during this incredibly difficult time,” said Captain Doreen McCarthy, the US Coast Guard sector New York commander. “We are extremely grateful for the heroic, swift actions of our partner agencies and Good Samaritan vessel who assisted in rescuing survivors from the water.” Associated Press contributed reporting Explore more on these topics New York US crime news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.michigandaily.com/statement/.text: Ella Flores Brosnan/DAILY “God punished man by taking away sleep and giving him knowledge.” — “On the Heights of Despair,” Emil Cioran Open, close. I was losing feeling in my fingers. In, out. My chest was perpetually tight, so I used brute force to mechanically breathe in two-second intervals, like pouring alcohol on an open wound. It’s near the end of the school day, and I’ve officially given up. I didn’t care if I had to miss class for a week if that’s what it would take: I needed to sleep. My junior year of high school had just started, and I didn’t know how I was going to survive. For three days, I barely slept, if at all. The year before, I began struggling with bouts of insomnia . While the COVID-19 pandemic raged on, it was easier to manage relentless fatigue while at home. I could even catnap at times. Now, I had to face in-person school, and this radical change made me a wreck. I was catastrophizing about every little detail, from friends to lunch to band to teachers to homework to sort-of friends to awkward encounters possibly related to dropping a pencil until it rolls too far so that you can’t smoothly pick it up but no one around will pick it up either to which seat you pick on the first day of class because everyone knows that unassigned assigned seats exist even if a teacher doesn’t enforce them. My insomnia just heightened these thoughts. However, the ultimate disaster would be not going to school at all because then everyone would forget about me. Obviously. I was positive that the entire school would witness some astonishing, life-altering event or form a lifelong bond I would miss out on. Anxiety works in interesting ways; I hated school, but I also couldn’t stand not going. Sometimes… Have you ever heard the term “dad lore” ? On a bright and sunny day, you’ll notice the birds chirping and a gentle breeze passing by, and your seemingly normal father will share an insane backstory as if he were merely discussing the weather. My dad is excellent at dropping dad lore, and he once told a gripping tale about a childhood friend. This friend’s dad, who worked for the United States embassy in Moscow, was captured and imprisoned in a Gulag — one of many labor camps that housed political prisoners from the 1920s to the 1950s in the Soviet Union. Inside, they tortured him with sleep deprivation, among other methods. Anytime he was found sleeping, a guard would kick him awake. With time, he learned to sleep flat on his stomach with one eye open, enough to fool the guards. Fast forward two decades, my dad stumbles into his friend’s house to find his father drinking at the dining room table with one eye squeezed shut and the other wide open like a hawk’s. Despite enduring one of the most traumatic sufferings possible, Alexander Dolgun was only paid $22,000 by the U.S. Embassy as compensation. He then wrote a book about his experience before his death in 1986. The less I sleep, the more I separate into two selves. Most people are familiar with Maslow’s hierarchy of needs. Put simply, without fulfilling physiological needs like air, food, shelter and rest, a person cannot think about the other needs that make up the rest of the pyramid — safety, love and belonging, esteem and self-actualization. When I don’t sleep, I can almost picture a transparent version of my soul detaching from my physical body until I am a hollow shell. Without my “true self,” that ghostlike soul controlling my body, my husk is governed by basic animalistic needs. Humans are animals, and the only thing differentiating us from that pigeon perched on a street lamp and that horse trotting across an open field is our intelligence and sense of self. I can feel myself regressing when I deprive myself of my most fundamental need — sleep — and I despise it. When I toss and turn at night, I wrestle with my thoughts, which often turn to Dolgun. And then the guilt sets in: How can I afford the luxuries of living in a comfortable situation in the Global North yet render myself incapable of basic rest? Just relax , my soul shrieks at my shell. Soothing, right? In high school, I knew this lifestyle was unsustainable. I would hyperfixate on the higher likelihood of drastic health issues caused by sleep deprivation: cancer, diabetes, heart disease, high blood pressure, fatal accidents, obesity, dementia, depression, anxiety — you’re even three times more likely to catch the common cold. If I couldn’t control my rest, I knew the path I would march towards: I am hunched over, poisoned into senselessness, carving my name on an early tombstone. Whatever basic solutions people have suggested to treat this problem, I’ve tried and even learned some things along the way. I’ve been to a sleep doctor, undergone a sleep study where professionals tracked my brain waves, done cognitive-behavioral therapy and taken sleep medication. The medication only provides a false feeling of sleepiness — a medically induced sedation — which did nothing to sway my mind into accepting the thick blanket of sleep. During the three-day ordeal in my junior year of high school, I somehow stayed awake despite taking a Tylenol PM, which is supposed to lull you into sleep. I could feel the onset of the sedative come and go, but it did nothing to ease the jitters that kept me awake. When your mind is your enemy, your battle tactics often fail. It is extremely difficult to find a permanent or foolproof solution to insomnia. After years of experimenting, I know that the way we go about fixing sleep deprivation is all wrong. We are constantly finding solutions to a symptom of the problem instead of attacking the problem itself. Insomnia is a rising global issue that’s mostly tied to privilege — or more specifically, lack thereof. Women, the elderly and people of lower socioeconomic backgrounds are more likely to suffer from insomnia, which contributes to the lack of attention on it. The National Center for Health Statistics found that in 2020, 8.4% of American adults had taken sleeping pills every day or most days within the past 30 days. Additionally, while people residing in industrialized regions — including the U.S. — experience longer and more efficient deep sleep, their circadian rhythms are substantially more disrupted than those in non-industrial societies. In an industrialized society, you will sleep around 45 minutes longer — the conditions for rest are optimized by things like air conditioning and high-quality mattresses— but experience significant circadian dysfunction, which is linked to a higher risk of inflammation, cancer, cardiovascular disease and mental health problems. I wish I could go into more detail about how I, specifically, was feeling in these moments, but truthfully, I have gaps in my memory from sheer lack of sleep. Whenever people talk about the “high school experience,” I feel mournful because I will never get those years back. I can’t even remember half of them. Even now, as a rising senior in college, there are sleep-deprived days when I walk around campus in a dazed shell, already severed into my two halves. I do everything in my power to hold myself together some days. I still feel insane jealousy for people who can fall asleep at the drop of a hat. Even worse is when people intentionally deprive themselves of sleep to cram for tests or other obligations, and then have the audacity to complain about it. The rage that consumes me is indescribable. They’re jumping around that stupid Maslow pyramid like it’s Chutes and Ladders, mistaking their needs for their wants. In 1934, Romanian philosopher Emil Cioran published “ On the Heights of Despair ,” inspired by his bouts of insomnia, depression and insanity. Cioran describes man as the “insomniac animal,” expressing that “there is not another animal in the entire creation that wants to sleep yet cannot.” He also finds offhanded, sarcastically written “blessings” of insomnia: “Insomnia kills off the multiplicity and diversity of the world, leaving you prey to your private obsessions. What strangely enchanted tunes gush forth during those sleepless nights!” That’s certainly one way to put it. I’m not sure I would agree with Cioran, as my “private obsessions” and “strangely enchanted tunes” more closely align with microsleeps , forgetfulness and hallucinations. There is some sort of mystique surrounding the archetype of the brilliant genius insomniac, similar to that of the starving artist. As if the world may never attribute their crazy habits as the source of their hidden superhuman intellect. But most people who have suffered from severe sleep problems understand the detachment of humanity that comes along with it. I’m done running around in circles trying to make sense of my nightly woes. My final thoughts might be unpopular and futile: Insomnia is pointless and downright stupid. It is a disease that has emerged as a side effect of humanity and our increased consciousness. So many questions remain. Are there truly insomniac babies, or are they just fussy? What baby — with the low intelligence and lack of consciousness that they possess — is contaminated by anxious thoughts and a restless mind? The mysteries of sleep may remain unsolved until the end of time, which may be the only thing that can provide me peace of mind. Photograph: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty Images Government borrowing Governments’ borrowing costs hit further multi-decade highs as US-Iran peace hopes fade Bond yields in US, UK, Germany France and Japan rise after ceasefire ends and Trump threatens to bomb Oman Business live – latest updates Julia Kollewe and Graeme Wearden Tue 18 Aug 2026 06.54 EDT Last modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 07.16 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Government borrowing costs continued to rise to levels not seen in decades on Tuesday, as hopes of an end to the US-Iran war faded. Concerns about the inflation outlook worsened after the ceasefire between Washington DC and Tehran ended on Monday night without an agreement , with no progress on the reopening of the strait of Hormuz. Donald Trump’s threat to bomb Oman if they “get in the way” of negotiations helped to push oil higher on Tuesday, to above $91 a barrel , and investors fear higher energy prices will push inflation up, leading to higher interest rates. Cooling UK labour market ‘questions need’ for Bank of England rate hikes; grocery inflation slows to two-year low – business live Read more Fiscal pressures are also rising as governments ramp up defence spending, which is expected to drive borrowing higher in leading European countries such as Germany and the UK. The yield, or interest rate, on the 30-year US Treasury bond rose to 5.324% on Tuesday, the highest since June 2007, adding to gains on Monday . The yield on the 10-year US Treasury bond rose to 4.736%, while the equivalent Japanese government bond yield climbed 2.5 basis points to 2.945%, the highest in three decades. The yield on the UK’s 10-year gilts rose 2.6bps to 5.076%. Germany’s 10-year bond yield rose to the highest level since 2011 while France’s equivalent hit a 16-year peak. Bond yields rise when the price of the debt falls. “Rising long-dated bond yields are not driven solely by expectations of higher interest rates and inflation fears. They can also reflect concerns around high levels of government borrowing and investors demanding greater compensation for the risks of holding long-dated government bonds,” Dan Coatsworth, the head of markets at AJ Bell, said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion Concerns about the amount of new debt hitting the bond markets, issued by governments and companies such as AI firms, is another factor pushing up yields. “We are seeing bond yields across developed markets strike multi-year highs as fixed income investors grow nervous about a range of factors, from inflation and the Iran conflict to deeper structural concerns and fiscal worries. Issuance is clearly a factor – both on the government side (they can’t stop spending!) and on the corporate side (AI capex),” said Neil Wilson, a Saxo UK investor strategist.
